The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1560 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • In a recent development, over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

In a recent development, over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern prepares the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

In a recent development, the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Recent findings suggest that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub problems made the fallback trainer risky.

Sources indicate that two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt indicates: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Sources indicate that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

According to recent reports, you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

According to recent reports, the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

Industry observers note that ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Industry observers note that training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

Industry observers note that no dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

In a recent development, paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

Recent findings suggest that it took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

In a recent development, ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

It has been revealed that if you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that reuters reported on November 26, 2026 that Dragos chief research officer HD Moore had identified MiniMax as the previously unnamed Chinese AI developer in a wider investigation of nearly two million seeded AI prompts. Researchers found private web links being opened later, including when consumers requested no storage or retention.

In a recent development, reuters said the public attribution and the Moscow-region findings were being reported for the first time. The evidence concerns particular URL fetches and later attempts to retrieve code; it does not establish that every prompt or model response sent to MiniMax was disclosed.

The November 19, 2026 research post described the method: prompts carried unique URLs and canary credentials, test secrets with no legitimate use, so later connections to controlled systems would reveal that someone had seen the original request. The testing ran from July through November 2026. For the then-unnamed lab, systems fetched secret URLs from more than half of prompts sent to its models between July and October 2026. The same happened to roughly two-thirds of requests marked no data collection or Zero Data Retention (ZDR), a setting intended to prevent storage of prompts and responses; fetches typically arrived two or three days later.

In a recent development, moore told Reuters that links sent through different providers were repeatedly opened from a Singapore internet connection. The pattern appeared when requests were forwarded to MiniMax’s cloud, not when other companies independently ran its models. For customers, that makes the hosting and forwarding path as consequential as the model they selected.

Recent findings suggest that one incident involving a link sent to MiniMax extended beyond automated fetching. The link appeared in a channel on Feishu, ByteDance’s workplace messaging platform, 24 days after the original prompt and was opened within two minutes on three desktops and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. Because Dragos had disclosed only the link’s first eight characters to the provider, the researchers inferred that whoever shared it had access to a stored copy of the full prompt.

In a recent development, researchers later observed attempts to clone private software repositories referenced in MiniMax requests. Reuters reported that the activity appeared after URL scraping seemed to stop on October 22, 2026; who initiated it and whether any code was obtained remain unclear. Researchers also detected unusual internet activity from the Moscow region involving links submitted to MiniMax, but the evidence did not establish that those links were opened from Russia.

MiniMax stated in a November 24, 2026 statement that its internal security system extracted URLs and IP addresses from forwarded web traffic into security logs for checks against threat intelligence. Automated security programs and agents subsequently probed some logged URLs. The monitoring was enabled by default on endpoints receiving forwarded requests and included traffic marked ZDR or no data collection.

MiniMax said the process recorded extracted addresses rather than full request or response content and did not retain full conversations. Its examination found no evidence that prompts or model responses were disclosed to third parties beyond the URL activity. The organization deleted the affected URLs, disabled the mechanism and verified that links were no longer opened on the identified path for current business-to-business traffic. The statement did not address the repository-download attempts or the Feishu incident.

According to recent reports, atlas Cloud stated in an updated security notice that MiniMax’s explanation matched its finding that links were opened after prompts reached MiniMax, not on Atlas Cloud infrastructure. The organization stopped forwarding requests to MiniMax’s official API and warned customers who used MiniMax M3, M2.7 or M3.1 Flash to treat submitted secrets as exposed and revoke affected credentials, tokens or links. Atlas had selected MiniMax’s Singapore data centers to avoid processing customer data in China, a choice that still left information potentially exposed after it reached MiniMax.

Novita remarked in a privacy notice that a routing-configuration issue sent some MiniMax requests to the official API instead of Novita-hosted infrastructure between May 28, 2026 and November 11, 2026. The affected paths included direct Novita traffic and requests routed through OpenRouter. The investigation found accesses to embedded URLs and hostnames, with no observed use of test markers for Amazon Web Services credentials. Novita advised customers whose requests contained live credentials or other secrets to revoke or rotate them.

Sources indicate that openRouter noted in a broader November 22, 2026 response that it had off-boarded three providers, removed 125 endpoints from ZDR eligibility and notified potentially affected customers. The platform found no breach or unauthorized access of OpenRouter itself; continuing work included adapting the researchers’ testing and verifying network paths.

Sources indicate that miniMax’s explanation accounts for the automated probes of logged links, while the Feishu sharing and repository-download attempts remain unattributed. The episode makes the full routing path central to AI privacy: no-retention settings did not stop systems along that path from extracting and later using embedded URLs.

Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

📅 13 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (576 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
  • Sources indicate that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

Sources indicate that LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

It has been revealed that for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

According to recent reports, serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

If you use this work, please cite the release blog:.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

At LINE BIZ CONVERGE 2026 on November 26, 2026, LINE Taiwan remarked it will pursue a three-part AI agent strategy spanning consumer assistance, brand service and merchant operations, building on more than 3.6 million official accounts to move customer interactions beyond answers toward completed tasks.

The strategy connects consumer access, brand fulfillment and merchant decision-making. It also places customer-facing agents within a broader product framework covering advertising, commerce and data, tying service interactions to subsequent business activity.

The planned Consumer Agent would handle everyday needs and connect users to services directly inside chats. Brand Agent, delivered through official accounts, would integrate brand service workflows and complete customer tasks. LINE Biz AI is the Business Agent, intended to combine data insights with operational recommendations and execution support for merchants.

Industry observers note that for brands, the upcoming AI agent platform will sit inside OA Plus, the administrative backend for official accounts. Businesses will be able to choose appointment, sales or customer-service agent roles and describe their requirements in natural language, with AI guiding the setup. They will also be able to combine basic and advanced functions according to their operating needs.

LINE Biz AI is designed to use the customer context created by those interactions. Within OA Plus, it would combine appointment records, product or service preferences, official-account interactions and membership information, automatically tag customer profiles and identify audiences. For a nail salon, that could mean recognizing a customer who has not booked recently, recommending a return-visit offer and sending messages when the merchant directs it to do so.

LINE first detailed the official-account platform in an October 13, 2026 announcement, which stated brands could connect their own point-of-sale, customer relationship management, membership, reservation and scheduling systems alongside standard templates. LINE planned to begin brand cooperation and validation at the end of 2026 and targeted a formal launch in the first quarter of 2027.

Sources indicate that LINE Biz AI has a separate, staged rollout. It became available on the LINE Biz-Solutions website in November 2026 to provide AI Q&A about products and services. LINE plans to bring it into OA Plus in the first half of 2027 for operational decision and action support, then gradually integrate AI capabilities across products in the second half of 2027 so it can assist across services.

The surrounding products are intended to connect agent interactions to transactions. The Chat Ad format in LINE’s LAP advertising system lets a consumer enter a brand conversation after clicking an ad and ask about a product or service before deciding whether to add the official account as a friend. A separate Cross Buy and LINE Gift test uses previous purchasing and gifting behavior to anticipate future gifting demand, generate ads from LINE Gift product assets and direct consumers back to LINE Gift to complete a purchase.

Physical stores provide another entry point. With LINE Touch, a shopper can tap a phone to open a brand’s LINE MINI App, collect coupons and redeem them in-store without downloading a separate app. LINE reports that a FamilyMart trial combining the two products reached a maximum coupon redemption rate of 91%.

For campaign planning, LINE Data Hub is designed to show audience profiles before ads run and use campaign results afterward to inform subsequent intends. AI Persona uses semantic analysis across LINE cross-service behavior labels, official-account friend data and user research, allowing brands to explore audience characteristics in natural language and receive suggestions for messaging and ad creative. LINE also plans partnerships under its DMP Alliance data program with Invoice Monster operator Chun Shu Technology, ECPay DATA and uTagGo to add spending, payment, ecommerce and mobility data sources.

Together, those products describe an operating loop in which an ad starts a conversation, an agent completes a service task and the resulting customer information informs the next action. With the main brand and merchant capabilities scheduled in stages through 2027, the practical test is whether those releases form a shared operating loop across OA Plus and LINE’s commerce and data tools, rather than a set of isolated chat features.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something newly introduced, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

In a recent development, pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

It has been revealed that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

In a recent development, add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Industry observers note that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Recent findings suggest that for edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

According to recent reports, everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

It has been revealed that A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

Recent findings suggest that A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

It has been revealed that this gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

Sources indicate that in stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Industry observers note that each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

In a recent development, text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps demonstrates how the image takes shape:.

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are fresh to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

Recent findings suggest that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Sources indicate that built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage Articles Engineering Reliable Telematics from Smartphone Sensors.

Nov 27, 2026 21 min read.

A smartphone can provide a surprising amount of information about a journey, including GPS estimates location and speed, accelerometers measure motion along the device's axes, gyroscopes capture rotation, and others. A connected vehicle may expose additional signals, such as speed, engine state, or diagnostic information.

Combining these sources creates opportunities for fleet monitoring, usage-based insurance, driving-behavior analysis, trip reconstruction, and connected mobility services.

However, having more sensors does not automatically produce better telemetry.

It has been revealed that find the bugs your tests miss. Antithesis uses deterministic simulation to explore thousands of failure scenarios, uncovering hard-to-reproduce bugs before they reach production. See how it works.

It has been revealed that in fact, a GPS enhancement may arrive after a vehicle has already slowed down. A phone may rotate in its mount, changing how its accelerometer readings relate to the vehicle's movement. An application may pause collection when the operating system restricts background activity. A backend service may receive observations out of order after a device reconnects.

Each observation may look reasonable in isolation, but the problem appears when the system combines observations that do not describe the same moment, coordinate frame, or physical event.

Recent findings suggest that I would approach this as an architectural problem before treating it as a sensor-processing problem. The goal is not to make every sensor perfect. It is to build a system that understands the limitations of its inputs and prevents unsuitable evidence from silently becoming a business decision.

In a recent development, this distinction matters because a misleading telemetry event can have consequences beyond an inaccurate chart. It may influence a driver's score, trigger a fleet alert, affect an insurance calculation, or lead an operations team to investigate an event that never happened as represented.

For architects, the challenge is deciding where sensor collection, normalization, quality evaluation, and event detection belong and what contracts connect those stages.

For mobile engineers, the concern is preserving useful observations despite changing device orientation, sampling gaps, intermittent connectivity, and operating-system lifecycle behavior.

For streaming and data engineers, the problem includes delayed events, out-of-order delivery, duplicate observations, and reconciling streams that operate at different sampling rates.

For product and operations teams, the question is how to distinguish a confident event from one that needs further evidence or should not be reported at all.

The practical outcome is a design approach that makes data limitations visible, keeps event logic separate from data-quality decisions, and provides evidence that can be inspected when a result is challenged.

I arrived at this architecture by tracing the journey of a telemetry observation from the moment it is captured to the point at which an application uses it to make a decision. Rather than starting with a sensor-fusion algorithm, I considered what could go wrong at each step. A speed measurement could be delayed, two observations could represent different moments, a phone's orientation could change, or an operating system interruption could leave gaps in the collected data. Each problem affects a different part of the processing flow, but all can ultimately influence the same business decision.

Sources indicate that this led me to identify the responsibilities that a reliable pipeline needs to address independently: preserving the original measurements, establishing their temporal relationship, interpreting them in a consistent reference frame, evaluating their quality, detecting events, and retaining the evidence behind the resulting decisions. These responsibilities form the six logical stages described below. The intent is not to prescribe a particular deployment topology, but to establish clear architectural boundaries so that uncertainty introduced at one stage does not silently propagate into the next.

It has been revealed that I prefer to separate raw measurement collection from interpretation. Requirements such as detecting harsh braking, classifying trips, or calculating a driving score should not dictate how raw observations are represented.

A practical architecture has six logical stages, as the following image highlights. They do not need to be six separately deployed services, as several can run within the same mobile application. The separation into six stages matters because each stage has a distinct responsibility, failure modes, and validation requirements. In the next sections, we are going to review all these stages in detail.

Figure 1. A quality-aware mobile telematics pipeline (Source: created by the author).

Start by retaining the original observation before applying transformations.

Industry observers note that A record should carry the value and its unit, source or sensor type, measurement timestamp, available arrival timestamp, and relevant metadata. Depending on the source, that metadata might include accuracy estimates, sensor sampling information, device identifiers, or the vehicle association.

Why preserve the original? Because a later transformation may be incorrect, an assumption may change, or an event may be disputed. If the system retains only its normalized output, engineers may be unable to determine whether the original observation was poor or the transformation introduced the error.

For example, suppose an application converts a GPS speed reading into a standardized unit and later combines it with vehicle speed. If an event looks implausible, the engineering team should be able to inspect the original value, its timestamp, and the conversion applied to it.

In a recent development, preservation does not mean keeping every field forever, since retention, privacy, security, and storage policies still apply. It means defining which evidence is needed for diagnosis and traceability before transformations discard it.

Sources indicate that sensor streams do not necessarily report at the same frequency or on the same schedule. A vehicle interface may produce frequent speed updates while GPS observations arrive less often. Mobile and backend components may also introduce different buffering and delivery delays.

The first distinction I make is between measurement time and arrival time.

Measurement time describes when the observation was captured, according to its source clock. Arrival time describes when a component received it. Arrival time is useful for understanding latency, but it is not a safe substitute for measurement time when reconstructing physical events.

According to recent reports, A stream processor that compares the latest values received from two sources can accidentally compare different moments. This becomes especially problematic during rapid acceleration, braking, or turning, when the underlying state changes rapidly.

The architecture should therefore define an alignment policy. It needs to specify how observations are matched, how much temporal separation is acceptable for each use case, and what happens when the system cannot find a suitable match.

Interpolation may be appropriate for some continuous signals, but it should not be applied indiscriminately. It can create a plausible-looking value where the evidence is sparse, and it may obscure a sharp change. The system should retain whether a value was directly measured, interpolated, or otherwise estimated.

When alignment cannot be established within the required tolerance, the right result may be lower confidence or no event at all.

It has been revealed that A measurement's value is only part of its meaning. Its unit, coordinate frame, source, and interpretation matter just as much.

A phone's accelerometer reports motion in device coordinates. Those axes are attached to the phone, not inherently to the vehicle. If the phone rotates in a mount, the relationship between the phone's axes and the vehicle's forward, lateral, and vertical directions changes.

A system that assumes the phone is always mounted in the same orientation can interpret device movement as vehicle movement. That can distort acceleration, braking, and turning estimates.

Recent findings suggest that normalization should make these assumptions explicit. It may include unit conversion, coordinate transformation, sensor calibration, and checks on the validity of orientation estimates. A transformed observation should retain enough information to identify the transformation and its assumptions.

The system must also distinguish coordinate normalization from measurement quality. A transformation can be mathematically correct but based on an uncertain orientation estimate. The result may therefore remain unsuitable for a particular event calculation.

At this stage, the system asks a different question: not simply whether a value exists, but whether it is fit for the intended use.

Useful checks include freshness, timestamp alignment, missing samples, source consistency, measurement uncertainty, and the reliability of any required coordinate transformation.

Sources indicate that these checks should not be buried inside individual event rules. A shared quality stage gives different event detectors a consistent view of the evidence and makes quality decisions easier to monitor and test.

I would use three broad outcomes:.

Recent findings suggest that these are not universal labels with fixed thresholds. A GPS observation might be adequate for a coarse trip map but unsuitable for calculating a short, sharp braking event. Quality must be evaluated in context.

Event detection should consume measurements that have already passed through the relevant quality checks.

Recent findings suggest that this does not mean every event requires every sensor. A trip-start detector and a harsh-braking detector have different evidence requirements. The architecture should allow each detector to declare what it needs and how it handles missing or uncertain inputs.

Consider a braking detector that combines vehicle speed and GPS speed. If the two values refer to different moments, the detector may infer a rate of deceleration that is not supported by the underlying movement. A quality-aware design prevents the detector from treating a poor match as equivalent to aligned observations.

The detector should also distinguish the event's classification from the quality of its evidence. An event may be a candidate for further review rather than a definitive result. Keeping these concepts separate makes the system easier to tune without changing the meaning of quality checks throughout the pipeline.

The final stage produces more than an event label.

In a recent development, A useful event record can include the event type, event time or interval, relevant vehicle or trip association, quality status, supporting observations, and the processing-rule version. Where a confidence estimate is used, its meaning and limitations should be documented rather than treating it as a universal probability of correctness.

Sources indicate that this information makes a decision inspectable. An engineer can trace an event to the observations that supported it, see whether any measurements were downgraded, and understand which processing logic was applied.

It also helps separate two questions that are often conflated: "What did the system decide?" and "What evidence justified that decision?".

According to recent reports, these six stages form one continuous data path. Raw preservation protects the evidence; temporal alignment and normalization make observations comparable; the quality gate determines their suitability; event detection applies the domain logic; and the final record explains the result.

The value of this architecture comes from the boundaries between stages.

Industry observers note that this is deliberately more than a sensor-fusion algorithm. It is a contract for how imperfect physical observations become software decisions.

The principle is straightforward: preserve what was measured, establish what it means, evaluate whether it is fit for use, and only then act on it.

Imagine a fleet operator whose mobile application scores driving behavior. Drivers receive alerts for harsh braking, and fleet managers use the events to identify potentially risky patterns.

Sources indicate that one morning, a driver approaches a traffic light and brakes normally. The smartphone collects GPS-derived speed while the vehicle interface reports speed independently. The backend later records a harsh-braking event.

The driver disputes the alert. The vehicle did slow down, but not as abruptly as the application claims.

Sources indicate that the engineering team examines the processing flow and discovers that the phone and vehicle streams were paired by arrival order. GPS updates were less frequent, and one observation represented an earlier point in the journey. During deceleration, the system compared that older speed estimate with a more recent vehicle measurement.

Industry observers note that the discrepancy looked like physical behavior. Part of it was actually a timing problem.

The pipeline had accepted both values because they were syntactically valid. It had no mechanism to establish whether they were temporally comparable.

Figure 2. How a timing mismatch can create a misleading event (Source: created by the author).

Industry observers note that the team introduces a temporal-alignment stage before event detection. Each observation retains its measurement timestamp, while arrival time is tracked separately. The pipeline evaluates the freshness of each observation and avoids comparing streams when timing uncertainty exceeds the application's defined tolerance.

The detector also stops treating every speed discrepancy as equivalent. When the measurements are not sufficiently aligned, it lowers confidence or abstains from generating a definitive event.

Sources indicate that the team adds monitoring for timestamp offsets, stale observations, alignment failures, and event reclassification. These metrics help distinguish a change in driving behavior from a change in data quality.

This approach does not guarantee that every braking event will be classified correctly. It gives engineers a way to identify a measurement-comparison problem before treating it as driver behavior.

The same pattern applies to fleet diagnostics, trip reconstruction, usage-based insurance, and connected-vehicle analytics.

The lesson: before interpreting disagreement between sensors as physical behavior, establish whether the measurements are temporally comparable.

Time alignment does not solve the second major problem: orientation.

Recent findings suggest that an accelerometer measures along the device's axes. A vehicle-relative interpretation assumes that the system knows how those axes relate to the vehicle. If the phone rotates, that relationship changes.

The gyroscope can help estimate rotation, and sensor-fusion algorithms can estimate orientation. Neither eliminates uncertainty automatically. Estimates may drift, the initial orientation may be unknown, and the phone can move independently of the vehicle.

A field named longitudinalAcceleration can therefore be misleading if it was calculated from device-relative measurements while the phone's orientation was uncertain.

The architecture should distinguish raw device-frame measurements from transformed estimates and preserve the assumptions behind each transformation.

Consider a mobile telematics application that detects cornering and sudden lateral movement using the phone's accelerometer and gyroscope.

Sources indicate that A driver starts a journey with the phone secured in a horizontal dashboard mount. The application estimates orientation and interprets motion relative to the vehicle. Later, the mount loosens on a rough road, and the phone rotates. The driver continues straight.

The application detects apparent lateral movement and records an aggressive-turning event.

The sensor values changed, but the physical interpretation was wrong. The device's orientation changed, so the relationship between its axes and the vehicle's direction of travel was no longer the same.

This problem is easy to miss when testing only with a phone mounted in a fixed position. The algorithm may perform well in a controlled setup and fail when people reposition the phone, adjust the mount, or carry it during a trip.

Recent findings suggest that figure 3. The device frame is not automatically the vehicle frame (Source: created by the author).

Industry observers note that the team makes orientation confidence an explicit input to event detection. Raw accelerometer and gyroscope observations are preserved, while transformed measurements carry metadata describing the estimated reference frame and the confidence in that transformation.

Industry observers note that the detector no longer assumes that one phone orientation remains valid for the entire journey. It monitors orientation changes and identifies periods when the relationship between the device and vehicle is uncertain.

Recent findings suggest that when orientation is reliable, the application can use transformed measurements according to its validated detection policy. When confidence falls, it can rely on other trustworthy evidence, reduce the confidence of the event, or abstain from making a definitive classification.

It has been revealed that the team tests deliberate phone rotations, loose mounts, different mounting positions, and periods when orientation cannot be estimated reliably. It measures false positives and false negatives against a defined reference rather than assuming that a more sophisticated algorithm automatically improves accuracy.

This also improves the user experience. Instead of penalizing a driver for an uncertain observation, the application can indicate that it could not classify the event reliably.

According to recent reports, the lesson: sensor accuracy and interpretation accuracy are different things. A sensor can report its measurement correctly while the application assigns that measurement the wrong physical meaning.

The same principle applies to phone-based activity recognition, wearable devices, robotics, and industrial IoT.

Sources indicate that the quality gate is the fourth stage in the architecture, but its responsibility extends beyond checking whether sensor values look reasonable. It determines whether the available measurements are reliable enough for the specific decision an application intends to make.

Recent findings suggest that the preceding stages preserve observations, establish temporal relationships, and normalize their measurement semantics. However, even after these steps, the resulting measurements may still contain uncertainty, missing samples, or inconsistencies. Without an explicit quality evaluation, individual event detectors must handle these conditions independently, often using different assumptions and fallback rules. This can lead to inconsistent decisions across the application.

I consider the quality gate a contract between the telemetry pipeline and the business logic that consumes its output. It makes the limitations of the available evidence explicit and defines what downstream components are permitted to do with it.

This section explores three aspects of that contract: why measurement quality must be evaluated in the context of the intended decision, how the system should distinguish between accepting, degrading, and abstaining from a result, and why abstention should be treated as a legitimate outcome rather than a processing failure.

Suppose a fleet application supports two functions: displaying the approximate route of a trip and identifying a short, aggressive braking maneuver.

According to recent reports, the route display may tolerate a less frequent location patch. The braking detector needs evidence that is sufficiently aligned in time and suitable for estimating a rapid change in speed.

Using the same universal threshold for both functions can be unnecessarily restrictive for one and dangerously permissive for the other.

It has been revealed that instead, each consumer should declare its requirements. The quality gate evaluates the observation against those requirements and communicates the outcome.

According to recent reports, this approach also makes product trade-offs explicit. If a team wants more events at the expense of accepting weaker evidence, that decision becomes a documented policy choice that can be evaluated—not an accidental consequence of a permissive fallback in a detector.

Engineering teams often focus on maximizing the number of events detected. But a system that always returns an answer can create a false sense of certainty.

Abstention is useful when the evidence does not support the intended decision. It should not be treated as an exception that disappears into a log file.

In a recent development, the system should record why it abstained, whether additional data could resolve the uncertainty, and whether the decision needs to be revisited. For some use cases, waiting briefly for a delayed observation is reasonable. For others, the system may need to return an explicit "insufficient evidence" outcome.

Recent findings suggest that this is especially important when events influence human decisions, scores, or downstream automation. A clearly identified lack of evidence is often more useful than a precise-looking result that cannot be defended.

In a recent development, A quality-aware architecture is only as good as the team's ability to see it working. If the system records only the number of events generated, it becomes difficult to distinguish a genuine change in driving behavior from a change in sensor availability, application lifecycle, or processing logic.

I would monitor the quality pipeline alongside the business outcomes.

Useful operational signals include:.

Recent findings suggest that these measurements should be segmented where useful by device type, operating-system version, sensor source, application version, and collection conditions. Otherwise, a system-wide average may conceal a failure affecting a particular group of devices.

I would also connect quality metrics to event outcomes. If the number of harsh-braking events suddenly rises, the team should be able to investigate whether driving behavior changed, timestamp skew increased, or a upcoming application version altered sampling behavior.

This requires a distinction between technical metrics and business metrics. Event counts and driver scores tell us what the application concluded. Freshness, alignment, and rejection metrics help explain whether the evidence behind those conclusions changed.

It has been revealed that observability should support investigation, not just dashboards. Logs and event records need enough structured context to reconstruct a decision while respecting data-retention and privacy requirements.

Sources indicate that A smartphone sensor pipeline does not run in a perfectly controlled environment. Applications can move into the background, devices can enter power-saving modes, connectivity can disappear, and operating systems can constrain background execution.

The architecture should not assume that a requested sampling rate guarantees a continuous stream.

On the device, collection code should handle sensor unavailability, sampling gaps, lifecycle transitions, and local buffering. When connectivity returns, queued observations may arrive in a burst or out of order. The backend should therefore apply its temporal-alignment and duplicate-handling policies even when the data originated from a single phone.

The system should preserve the distinction between the time an observation was measured and the time it was uploaded. It should also make gaps visible rather than filling them silently with fabricated continuity.

Recent findings suggest that offline operation introduces another design decision: how much data to buffer and for how long. That depends on the product's latency, privacy, storage, and battery constraints. Not every observation needs to be retained indefinitely, but the policy should be deliberate.

Industry observers note that these concerns are not separate from sensor reliability. They determine whether the system has enough timely evidence to make a defensible decision.

Industry observers note that I would not attempt to perfect every sensor or event detector at once. I would start with one high-impact event and establish a reliable path through the architecture.

According to recent reports, the goal is not to add complexity for its own sake. It is to discover where the system's assumptions are hidden and make them explicit before those assumptions affect a business decision.

A quality-aware architecture makes sensor limitations and processing uncertainty explicit, but it does not eliminate them. Architects and developers should consider several limitations when applying this model.

The architecture can identify missing samples, stale observations, and unreliable measurements, but it cannot reconstruct physical events when evidence was never captured. Interpolation and estimation may help, but introduce assumptions and should not be treated as direct measurements. When evidence is insufficient, the system should communicate that limitation rather than manufacture continuity.

In a recent development, the six stages define architectural responsibilities, not specific sensor-fusion, calibration, or event-detection algorithms. Developers must validate these techniques against appropriate reference measurements and real-world conditions. A well-structured pipeline cannot compensate for an inaccurate orientation estimate or an incorrectly designed detection algorithm.

Sources indicate that freshness, timestamp tolerance, measurement uncertainty, and orientation confidence must be evaluated against the intended decision. Requirements for displaying a trip route differ from those for detecting harsh braking. Thresholds should be validated for each use case, and confidence scores should not be treated as universal probabilities of correctness.

Recent findings suggest that background execution restrictions, battery consumption, connectivity, device diversity, and privacy influence what can be collected and processed. Teams must balance these constraints with evidence requirements and processing latency. They must also define how uncertain outcomes and abstentions are communicated and when additional data or manual review is appropriate.

In a recent development, ultimately, this architecture is a framework for managing uncertainty, not a guarantee of perfect telemetry. Its effectiveness depends on sensor quality, validated algorithms, appropriate quality requirements, and continuous testing under real-world conditions.

Recent findings suggest that smartphones make telematics more accessible by combining location, motion sensors, computing power, and connectivity in a single device. But the convenience comes with a trade-off: device placement varies, sampling behavior is managed by the mobile platform, and measurements have different timing and coordinate semantics.

The architectural response is to separate observation from interpretation. Preserve what the phone measured. Establish when and in what frame it was measured. Evaluate whether the evidence is suitable for the decision. Only then should business logic act on the result.

It has been revealed that the phantom braking scenario shows why measurements from different sources must be temporally comparable. The rotated-phone scenario shows why device orientation must be treated as a variable rather than an assumption. Both demonstrate why a technically healthy pipeline can still produce an unreliable conclusion.

The distinction is simple: collecting telemetry produces data. Engineering reliable telemetry produces evidence that downstream systems can evaluate, qualify, and use responsibly.

Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing

1. Why is email marketing important?Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.2. What is benefits of email marketing?Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:Better brand recognitionStatistics of what works bestMore salesTargeted audienceMore traffic to your products/services/newsletterBuild credibilityMost  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide. 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.5. How do I write a decent subject line?The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free. 6. Is email marketing still effective?Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience. 7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them. 8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also revision them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your people' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.10. Where can I find email template?Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use. However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.Final Saying You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something newly introduced and different to deal with as you market your own business.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

WaterSense unveiled on November 26, 2026 that it had raised a combined €5.75 million in pre-seed investment and grants to expand AI-supported water-quality monitoring across Europe, including a proposal to monitor the Oder River continuously from its sources to its mouth.

Recent findings suggest that the pre-seed round was co-led by b2venture and Movens Capital, with participation from vastpoint. The announcement separately identifies €3.5 million from Poland’s National Centre for Research and Development for further sensor development and satellite-data integration. That work is intended to add measurements for ammonium ions, nitrates, orthophosphates, fluorides, lead and E. coli, extending analysis from individual stations to entire water bodies and watercourses.

WaterSense is addressing a monitoring gap created by manual sampling: field teams collect water at individual sites and send it to laboratories, producing accurate results that can arrive days later and describe only past conditions. Its model replaces those isolated readings with continuously operating autonomous stations connected to a cloud analytics platform, giving utilities, industrial operators and public authorities a current view of rivers, lakes and industrial water systems.

The hardware uses hundreds of inexpensive miniature printed sensors, automatically replaced inside the station instead of relying on one expensive sensor that must remain stable through long exposure. WaterSense says this limits the impact of biofouling, the buildup of aquatic organisms on equipment, and reduces servicing needs. The sensor design originated in founder Filip Budny’s doctoral research at Warsaw University of Technology.

WaterSense’s product description lists more than 25 water-quality parameters measured every ten minutes. The stations use hybrid solar and optional hydro power, supporting continuous operation without cables or external power infrastructure.

According to recent reports, field readings create a growing reference database connected to satellite observations and deep-learning models. WaterSense notes the models can forecast water-quality changes up to 72 hours ahead and that AI agents turn the combined data into alerts, operational conclusions and decision support. The operational goal is earlier warning for intake protection and better-informed treatment decisions.

According to recent reports, the ASIR research project, which is developing an autonomous Internet of Things system for water-quality monitoring and threat identification, runs from September 1, 2024 through August 30, 2027. Alongside the station, it includes cloud-based anomaly detection and an interactive national river-pollution risk map for planning measurements and station placement. Warsaw University of Technology leads a consortium whose other members are the Institute of Meteorology and Water Management, MAGLY and NEBUCODE.

WaterSense reports monitoring more than 80 points for over 30 customers in four European countries. Its customers include industrial operators, large water utilities, cities and regional authorities. They receive continuous measurements, alerts, analysis and decision-support tools through a Data-as-a-Service subscription, under which WaterSense supplies the monitoring infrastructure and customers avoid building their own field teams and measurement systems.

Deployments include alpine lakes in Austria and urban water systems in large European cities. In Kitzbühel, Austria, the monitored parameters include water temperature, conductivity, pH, dissolved oxygen and phycocyanin, a pigment that serves as a blue-green algae indicator. The continuous view is intended to help local teams track changes between field visits and plan environmental stewardship and tourism activities.

The upcoming capital is intended to move WaterSense beyond individual installations toward a denser monitoring network across European rivers, lakes and water systems. WaterSense says each deployment adds to a geographically varied reference dataset and strengthens its predictive analytics. The Oder project would extend continuous observation and decision support from selected locations to the full length of the river.

In a recent development, the announcement cites the 2022 ecological crisis along hundreds of kilometres of the Oder, which affected water utilities and river-dependent businesses, as an example of decisions being made with information that arrives too late. The planned river-wide deployment gives the company’s network model a concrete test: consistent field measurements and useful forecasts would need to support decisions across connected stretches of water, where pollution can affect owners far beyond an individual monitoring point.
