#229956. How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 11m • 📚 Deep Dive (2215 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications

📅 21 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2215 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.
  • In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens.
  • Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications.

In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model.

Industry observers note that the tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step.

Recent findings suggest that one of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency.

Recent findings suggest that the model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses.

We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication.

Industry observers note that the leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense.

For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once.

It has been revealed that the first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request.

The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses.

According to recent reports, the natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill.

Recent findings suggest that to see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill, the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode, the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth.

This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading.

Sources indicate that think of a shipping firm that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings.

The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model.

It has been revealed that and the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows.

Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a fresh idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations.

In a recent development, they choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve.

Industry observers note that they work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one.

VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first.

In a recent development, first, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly.

Industry observers note that second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping firm: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget.

To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points.

Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain.

An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated.

A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running.

That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%.

Sources indicate that to measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime.

Industry observers note that the model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810.

It has been revealed that getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version.

Recent findings suggest that the lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter.

To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling.

VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803.

Sources indicate that vocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe.

Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary.

The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon.

The Scaling Problem No One Talks About in Education: Who Checks the Teacher?

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 newly introduced children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.
  • It has been revealed that frankly, he asked me the right question.
  • Industry observers note that most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I remember when we started discussing a major venture round to open up 30 newly introduced children’s clubs a year, one investor’s question stuck with me: “How will you keep the quality of teaching the same in location number 30 as in location number one?”.

It has been revealed that frankly, he asked me the right question. In education, scale is rarely limited by capital, real estate, or demand. It’s instead limited by the one thing that is hardest to copy: what actually happens between a teacher and a group of children when no one is checking?

Industry observers note that most education networks control quality the way they did 30 years ago. A supervisor visits the site, sits in on a class, and takes notes. Then, someone else watches a recording later. It works at three locations, but this could be broken at the last branch.

Let me explain this using GMNSM as an example. Take 10 locations, with four groups a day at each, six days a week. At 30 minutes of review per session, that adds up to 480 review hours over four weeks. Using our own staffing costs for manual reviews, I estimate that would cost about US$6,100. The estimated workload grows with every club you add. Sampling keeps that workload down, but it leaves most lessons unseen.

The lesson for education is straightforward: if you can only inspect a sliver of what happens, you are not managing quality, but guessing at it.

According to recent reports, speech AI has become good enough, and cheap enough, to turn a lesson recording into something a manager can act on. The research is also catching up. In a pre-registered randomized controlled trial with 224 Utah mathematics and science teachers, automated feedback on classroom audio increased teachers’ use of focusing questions by 20% compared with a control group.

Commercial tools are following now as well. Coverage in Education Next describes apps that separate teacher and student speech, and reports talk time and wait time, “like a Fitbit for instruction.” However, the same piece also raises the hard question: what happens when this data moves from private reflection into a formal evaluation?

At GMNSM, we built Allim AI, an internal system to automate this quality loop, and the process was more instructive than the technology.

Industry observers note that the idea is simple. You give the model your methodology – values, annual programme, lesson structure, and expected outcomes. The system reviews the coach’s speech in the discussion after practice, not the training session itself. It checks which questions the coach asked against the lesson plan and flags moments that may warrant human review. If the lesson is about building confidence, we ask: “did the coach discuss the assigned video, ask the required questions, summarize the takeaways, and help children apply them to real life?”.

The output is a score and practical coaching notes: fewer filler words, less judgemental language, and more room for different perspectives instead of one “correct” answer.

Three design decisions mattered more to us than the model itself.

According to recent reports, not everyone welcomed this in GMNSM. Some colleagues left because mandatory microphones felt like we didn’t trust them. I understand their reaction, and I would even be suspicious of any founder who dismisses it.

The wider data says this is not an edge case. Gallup research found that only 20% of employees who work on a computer or digital device have a great deal of trust in their leaders to use employee data responsibly. A 2025 ExpressVPN survey found that one in six employees had considered quitting over monitoring they considered invasive. As one expert put it in a recent HR Daily Advisor-style analysis of AI that detects toxic managers, the same tool can look like support in a high-trust organization and “Massive Brother” in a low-trust one.

So, my practical advice to other operators is this: treat it as a development tool first. If staff only ever see it as a scoreboard, they’ll either game it or leave. If it gives them specific, private, useful feedback, many will start using it the way it’s intended to be used. Tell people what gets recorded, why, and who sees it before it goes out. Also, accept that some people will opt out. When we did this, we explained the purpose to some colleagues and parted ways with others, which we respect.

Recording children’s classes raises obvious data-protection questions, and in Europe, the rulebook is tightening. Under the EU AI Act, certain uses of AI in education and employment can be classified as high-risk, depending on the system’s intended purpose. Not every use falls into that category, but the direction of travel is clear: the more an AI system influences decisions about people, the more scrutiny it should expect.

Whatever the legal classification, the practical principles are the same. Disclose what is recorded and who can access it. Minimize the data you collect. Keep people, not algorithms, responsible for decisions. These practices help earn the trust that makes feedback at scale possible.

Sources indicate that finally, AI will not fix a weak methodology, and it cannot replace a coach who genuinely cares about children. What it can do is make quality visible, consistently and affordably, so the lesson in location number 30 is no more of an accident than the lesson in location number one.

Andrej Kuprejev is the founder and CEO of GMNSM, a Dubai-based martial arts and holistic education network, and the founder of Allim.AI, the AI platform that supports coaching quality across its academies. A Lithuania-born former competitive judo and jiu-jitsu athlete, he founded GMNSM in 2022 to combine physical training with soft-skills development for children. It now runs 11 academies across the UAE, Qatar and Cyprus.

Breaking: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3105 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done.
  • We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome.
  • ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that this is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Mentioned It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

In a recent development, figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Recent findings suggest that each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+.

Sources indicate that so we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

Sources indicate that we used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Recent findings suggest that table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

Sources indicate that thinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly latest solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

Recent findings suggest that if you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 reveals which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

In a recent development, table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

Recent findings suggest that the headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

It has been revealed that average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20.

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:.

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

According to recent reports, figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

In a recent development, the move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

It has been revealed that the dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

According to recent reports, selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Recent findings suggest that every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

In a recent development, training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

In a recent development, zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:.

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Sources indicate that why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++.

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

Industry observers note that so we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:.

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½).

In a recent development, figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:.

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO enhancement.

In a recent development, figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In a recent development, in the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

Two reward paths, one binary verdict.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:.

In a recent development, tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

Industry observers note that the public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Keep the three repositories side by side:.

The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock:.

The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel.

In a recent development, start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:.

Citing several media reports, Greenpeace Belgium remarked on November 27, 2026 that the Walloon Region had ordered construction stopped at Google’s Aiseau-Presles data-center site on November 26, 2026, after the group sought an emergency halt over work continuing despite the amended permit’s revocation.

In a recent development, the reported order followed Greenpeace’s November 23, 2026 letter to the Walloon administration requesting an immediate stop. Residents had alerted the group that work was continuing, and its emergency-procedure release indicates satellite imagery supported the request. Spokesperson Nadia Cornejo welcomed the reported stoppage and noted Greenpeace would continue monitoring activity at Aiseau-Presles.

Google’s original permit, granted in 2024, covered three data centers. A revised application in 2025 merged two of them into a single larger building and replaced the planned air-cooling system with water cooling drawn from the Sambre, making water use central to the subsequent permit dispute.

The Walloon administration approved the amended permit in April 2026, and residents appealed a month later. Walloon minister François Desquesnes revoked it in August 2026 following that appeal. Greenpeace connected the decision with what it described as a historic drought in Belgium and said the minister had highlighted the data center’s water needs in his reasoning.

In a recent development, the satellite document supporting the suspension request contains five observation dates between August 13, 2026 and November 14, 2026. As a comparison for the cooling demands at problem, Greenpeace notes Google’s existing Saint-Ghislain project withdraws 1 billion liters of water annually for cooling, returns one-quarter of it and evaporates the remainder.

According to recent reports, the site is part of the Écopole business park, which covers more than 150 hectares across Farciennes and Aiseau-Presles on rehabilitated industrial land. The municipality records the first-stone ceremony for the Google data center on April 5, 2024.

Greenpeace’s account of the Council of State proceedings claims Google sought annulment and suspension of the revocation on October 17, 2026. Greenpeace and several residents sought to intervene on November 16, 2026 to present their arguments, and a public hearing is scheduled for January 7, 2027.

Separately, a Walloon government framework published on November 12, 2026 presents data centers as support for AI and cloud development while identifying electricity, land and water as strategic constraints. The framework makes a prior partnership contract with the region a condition for covered projects with capacity of at least 25 megawatts, excluding infrastructure exclusively for an organization’s own needs.

The framework relies on existing authorization procedures rather than creating a fresh one. It also bars data centers from sites meeting regional strategic-location criteria, subject to stated exceptions, and calls for projects to document electricity demand and ramp-up intends while setting expectations for water efficiency and recovery of waste heat.

The immediate question is whether construction remains stopped while Google’s legal challenge proceeds. Wallonia’s wider framework makes the underlying trade-off explicit: attracting AI and cloud investment while preserving electricity, strategic industrial land and water for residents and other businesses.

  • Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

InfoQ Homepage News Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes.

Nov 27, 2026 2 min read.

Netflix has developed Quasar, an internal tool that identifies which repositories use specific library API symbols, helping engineering teams assess the downstream impact of proposed changes before releasing them. The tool combines semantic code indexing with API comparisons to identify affected consumers, dependency versions, and relevant call sites across repositories.

Industry observers note that the challenge extends beyond identifying whether an API change is incompatible. Compatibility tools can flag a removed method or changed signature, but they do not necessarily identify which applications call it. Dependency graphs show declared relationships rather than actual usage, while text searches can miss references involving inheritance, overloads, and generated code. Building every downstream consumer to validate a change can also be expensive.

Quasar architecture diagram showing the indexing and query workflow (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

Industry observers note that quasar indexes symbol definitions and references using the SCIP Code Intelligence Protocol, an open format for representing code relationships. Language-specific indexers submit data during CI builds, which Quasar stores in Amazon S3 as Parquet files and queries through Amazon Athena.

It has been revealed that during pull request analysis, Quasar compares API definitions between commits and identifies added, removed, or modified symbols. It then queries indexed references to locate affected repositories, dependency versions, and source locations. A Netflix example shows a deprecated method removal affecting 137 repositories across three library versions.

Example Quasar impact report showing affected repositories and dependency versions (Source: Netflix Blog Post).

Recent findings suggest that however, an absence of indexed references does not prove that an API is unused. Reflection, dynamic loading, stale indexes, and incomplete coverage can prevent Quasar from observing every consumer.

Recent findings suggest that antonio J. del Águila, founder of Knaisoma, highlighted another limitation in a LinkedIn discussion about the approach:.

Observed usage has a blind spot for reflection and for code on rare paths, like a quarterly batch job, since those calls may never show up in the window that was sampled.

Roberto Pérez Alcolea, a member of Netflix's Java Platform Team and author of the original article, acknowledged the limitation and described ongoing work to complement static evidence:.

Industry observers note that reflection and incomplete indexing remain blind spots, and we’re also investing in runtime analysis to complement the static evidence. Together, those signals help inform removal decisions, without guaranteeing that an API is safe to delete.

Quasar complements Revapi for API compatibility analysis and Kythe for code navigation by connecting API changes with actual usage across repositories. SCIP supports usage queries across Java, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust, while compatibility analysis covers JVM APIs and Protobuf changes traced through generated Java code. Netflix exposes findings through REST, GraphQL, and a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server for developers and coding agents.

In a recent development, netflix intends to move impact analysis earlier into coding workflows, allowing agents to identify public API changes and retrieve consumer information before pull requests are opened. The goal is to help prepare migration changes while keeping API and release decisions with library producers.

  • The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

In a recent development, the torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We proposal to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:.

No need for torchrun: the script debuts its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

According to recent reports, A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:.

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel blueprint use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

In a recent development, at the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS indicates nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space highlights comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:.

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, trueLayer confirmed on November 27, 2026, that a Papa John’s AI agent had completed what it described as the first agentic Pay by Bank payment to a named UK retailer. The pilot involved UK retail banks including Lloyds and NatWest and ran through the Financial Conduct Authority’s Supercharged Sandbox.

The agent helped with the customer’s order and then paid directly from the bank account linked to the customer’s Papa John’s account. Pay by Bank uses open-banking technology to link a bank account rather than a card, bringing the payment step into the AI-assisted ordering process. At a showcase on November 26, 2026, TrueLayer presented its findings to the FCA and industry participants.

Recent findings suggest that A customer creates one mandate with the bank, setting limits for a particular merchant or over a chosen period that the agent cannot exceed. Each attempted payment is checked against those limits, so an instruction above them is declined by the bank rather than relying on the agent to police itself. Payment approval remains inside the bank app, keeping banking credentials and passwords away from the agent. Customers can revoke the arrangement through either the merchant or their banking app at any time.

This separates the agent’s ability to initiate a purchase from the bank’s enforcement of the customer’s payment authority. TrueLayer also described the pilot as the first agentic use of the variable recurring payment APIs at Lloyds and NatWest, bank interfaces for payments authorized under an ongoing customer mandate.

TrueLayer argues that bank mandates let consumers delegate purchases without sharing card details, that non-card payments can preserve competition in payment acceptance as agents handle more shopping, and that the showcase can inform the conditions and standards needed for safe adoption at scale. The work remains a sandbox pilot rather than a general consumer launch.

Industry observers note that the retailer pilot followed TrueLayer’s July 22, 2026 announcement of its selection for the sandbox. The FCA received 199 applications and selected 21 companies for a cohort running from July 13, 2026, through December 31, 2026, with a particular focus on agentic payments. The sandbox, part of the FCA’s AI Lab, provides a controlled setting and regulatory support for moving advanced AI use cases toward commercial deployment.

Industry observers note that an earlier prototype kept a person in the loop while completing a transaction inside an AI shopping agent. It supported a one-off immediate payment and Bank on File, which establishes a recurring mandate for future purchases. The Papa John’s work extends those mechanics into a named retailer’s ordering flow with participating UK banks.

The FCA’s expectations for agentic AI in financial services, published on November 24, 2026, add regulatory context to the demonstration. The regulator said firms must identify which agent activities require authorization and which rules apply, particularly when software can initiate transactions, move money, arrange borrowing or make investment decisions.

Using an external AI provider does not transfer compliance responsibility away from a regulated firm or its senior managers. They are expected to understand how autonomously their systems act, the risks created and the controls needed in real time and under stress. When customers’ agents approach a firm, it should have processes to recognize the agent, verify consent and permitted actions, and provide help if something goes wrong.

According to recent reports, payments are a specific case. Before accepting an agent’s instructions, firms should assess their systems, controls and potential liabilities, including whether to accept a payment initiated by an AI agent or from a wallet under its control. The pilot’s bank-held mandate and in-app approval address the spending-control portion of that assessment; they do not by themselves settle broader questions of regulatory authorization, liability and senior-management oversight.

The pilot establishes a concrete division of authority between agent and bank. Wider adoption depends on pairing that payment mechanism with the FCA’s broader expectations for accountability, consent, liability and customer support, which extend beyond whether an individual transaction stays within its limit.

The $30,000 average wedding figure you see everywhere is misleading. That number is skewed upward by luxury weddings in expensive metros like New York, San Francisco, and Los Angeles. The national median — the number where half of weddings cost more and half cost less — sits closer to $10,000 to $15,000. That distinction matters because it means a beautiful, memorable wedding is absolutely possible without spending five figures you do not have.

In a recent development, the FI perspective adds another layer: every dollar spent on a wedding is a dollar that cannot compound for decades. A $30,000 wedding invested for 30 years at a 7% average annual return grows to roughly $228,000. That does not mean you should elope in a courthouse (unless you want to), but it does mean you should spend intentionally on the categories that matter most to you and cut ruthlessly everywhere else.

Sources indicate that not all wedding spending creates equal memories. Research consistently demonstrates that couples remember three things most vividly years later: the ceremony itself, the food and drinks, and the photographs. Almost nobody remembers the chair covers, the napkin folds, or the custom monogram on the cocktail napkins.

That insight creates a clear FI-aligned strategy: splurge on what creates lasting memories (photographer, food, music) and minimize everything else.

According to recent reports, the golden rule of wedding budgeting: if you cannot remember whether a detail was present at the last three weddings you attended, your guests will not notice either. Cut it without guilt.

The biggest financial mistake couples make is not setting a firm budget before visiting any vendors. Venues and vendors are skilled at upselling, and without a hard number in mind, costs spiral quickly. Start with a number you can pay in cash — wedding debt is one of the worst ways to begin a marriage and a direct threat to your FI timeline.

Follow this payment timeline to manage cash flow without credit card debt:.

Sources indicate that A practical savings strategy: divide your total budget by the number of months until the wedding and automate that transfer to a dedicated savings account. If your budget is $15,000 and your wedding is 15 months away, that is $1,000 per month. Treat it like any other savings goal on your FI path — automate, do not touch, and watch it grow.

For couples on the FI path, consider this reframe: every dollar you shave from the wedding budget is a dollar that starts compounding immediately. Cutting $5,000 from a $20,000 wedding and investing that savings at 7% for 25 years creates roughly $27,000 in future wealth. You can have a wonderful wedding and build wealth simultaneously — but only if you proposal intentionally from the start.

According to recent reports, before finalizing your wedding budget, run the compound interest math on any amount you are considering spending. A $30,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $228,000. A $15,000 wedding invested at 7% for 30 years becomes roughly $114,000. This is not an argument against celebrating — it is an argument for spending intentionally on what matters to you and cutting everything else. The couple who spends $15,000 on a joyful celebration and invests the other $15,000 gets both the wedding and a significant head start on financial independence.

Sources indicate that there is no single right number, but the median US wedding cost of $10,000 to $15,000 is achievable for most couples without going into debt. Focus on what matters most to you and cut everything else. A $10,000 wedding with great food, a good photographer, and people you love is better than a $30,000 wedding that starts your marriage with financial stress.

According to recent reports, no. Wedding debt is one of the worst forms of consumer debt because it funds a single day with no residual asset value. The average couple who finances their wedding on credit cards at 22% interest turns a $20,000 wedding into a $28,000 expense over 4 years of payments. Set a cash budget and stick to it.

In a recent development, any contribution from parents is a gift, not an obligation. If parents offer to contribute, have an honest conversation about the total amount and whether it comes with expectations about the guest list or style. Budget based on what you can afford independently, then treat any parental contribution as a bonus.

It has been revealed that yes. Friday and Sunday weddings typically cost 20-30% less than Saturday weddings for the same venue and vendors. Some venues offer discounts of 40% or more for weekday weddings (Monday through Thursday). Off-season months like January, February, March, and November also offer significant savings.

Tips for vendors (plan 15-20% for catering staff, bartenders, and drivers), alterations for wedding attire ($200-$500), marriage license fees ($30-$100), and overtime charges if the reception runs past the contracted time. Build a 10% contingency buffer into your total budget for these surprises.

Set your budget privately as a couple before discussing with family. Present it as a decision, not a discussion. If family members want upgrades, they are welcome to fund those specific additions. Protect your financial foundation — the marriage matters more than the wedding, and starting debt-free sets up your partnership for success.

In a recent development, A meaningful wedding does not require $30,000 or any specific dollar amount. Set a cash budget based on what you can afford without debt, allocate spending toward what creates lasting memories (food, photography, people), and cut everything else. Every dollar you save on the wedding is a dollar that starts compounding toward your financial independence. The couples with the strongest financial futures are the ones who celebrate joyfully within their means and invest the difference.

Industry News: Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1276 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is our newly introduced generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence.
  • LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.
  • Sources indicate that LFM2 demonstrated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that LFM3 is our newly introduced generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:.

Sources indicate that LFM2 demonstrated that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:.

Sources indicate that the payoff highlights at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two newly introduced in-house encoders:.

According to recent reports, each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Sources indicate that reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:.

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:.

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a newly introduced in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:.

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:.

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:.

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Recent findings suggest that reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:.

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:.

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:.

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:.

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

Aditya Infotech Completes KGraph Stake Deal for AI Surveillance

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Unite

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Aditya Infotech Limited mentioned in a stock-exchange filing on November 27, 2026 that it had completed a ₹45.39 crore cash purchase of 30% of KGraph AI Solutions Private Limited on a fully diluted basis.
  • The company’s November 5, 2026 announcement described the consideration as a mix of fresh equity and purchases from existing shareholders, with an implied post-money valuation of approximately ₹151 crore.
  • According to recent reports, the price was based on a registered valuer’s report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Aditya Infotech Limited mentioned in a stock-exchange filing on November 27, 2026 that it had completed a ₹45.39 crore cash purchase of 30% of KGraph AI Solutions Private Limited on a fully diluted basis. KGraph becomes an associate manufacturer, with its BLUE video-analytics technology slated for integration into CP PLUS surveillance products.

The company’s November 5, 2026 announcement described the consideration as a mix of fresh equity and purchases from existing shareholders, with an implied post-money valuation of approximately ₹151 crore. Managing Director Aditya Khemka noted: “Video compression is foundational to the next phase of surveillance. As cameras multiply and resolutions rise, the cost of storing and moving video becomes the real constraint.”.

According to recent reports, the price was based on a registered valuer’s report. The transaction was not a related-party deal, none of Aditya Infotech’s promoters, promoter group or group companies had an interest in KGraph, and no governmental or regulatory approvals were required.

According to recent reports, KGraph’s Semantic Codec adds a perception-aware compression layer to the standard H.264 video codec, identifying redundant visual information while retaining essential details. Based on deployment data, Aditya Infotech stated the technology could reduce video storage and bandwidth requirements by up to 90%.

It has been revealed that the codec is designed for cost-efficient edge hardware without GPU infrastructure and works with existing cameras and recording systems. The manufacturer noted this could extend video retention and lower deployment costs without replacing installed infrastructure, giving CP PLUS a potential upgrade path for customers already running surveillance equipment.

In a recent development, KGraph’s broader BLUE platform turns continuous video streams into searchable enterprise data. The investment is part of CP PLUS 2.0, Aditya Infotech’s move from hardware-led surveillance toward integrated security covering data management, edge computing, AI analytics and cloud integration.

KGraph will continue to operate independently while collaborating with Aditya Infotech’s R&D and engineering teams in Noida, Ahmedabad and Taiwan. The collaboration pairs KGraph’s computer-vision, embedded-systems and compression expertise with Aditya Infotech’s engineering, manufacturing and customer reach.

Sources indicate that KGraph’s six co-founders bring 15 to more than 20 years of experience and academic backgrounds from IIT Bombay and IIM Bangalore. The firm has a 10-patent pipeline, with three applications filed and seven in progress.

Incorporated on August 16, 2023, KGraph develops AI-powered software for compliance, automation, safety, monitoring and regulatory reporting across industrial and commercial sectors. It operates in India, and BLUE is its principal product.
