Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1976 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up quickly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Sources indicate that token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

Sources indicate that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

Recent findings suggest that this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

In a recent development, for example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Sources indicate that even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

Recent findings suggest that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

It has been revealed that hierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

According to recent reports, these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

Recent findings suggest that with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

Recent findings suggest that adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Recent findings suggest that rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

If you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

Industry observers note that the first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives enhancement the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

It has been revealed that cachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

In a recent development, gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

Recent findings suggest that multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

Recent findings suggest that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

The complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

Recent findings suggest that the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

You can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

The default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

According to recent reports, the pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

Sources indicate that I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

Industry observers note that at the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

The gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

It has been revealed that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

It has been revealed that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Recent findings suggest that try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

According to recent reports, with a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

Blockchain technology provides a way of avoiding this situation by using multiple computers at different locations to store information about transactions. If one computer experiences problems with a transaction, it will not affect the other nodes.

Instead, other nodes will use the correct information to cross-reference your incorrect node. This is called “Decentralization,” meaning all the information is stored in multiple places.

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

In a recent development, tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

Industry observers note that building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps customers entirely in control of their digital lives.

BotPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

Sources indicate that we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

In a recent development, next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

Recent findings suggest that finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

The second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

According to recent reports, botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

It has been revealed that tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

It has been revealed that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

It has been revealed that botPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

Table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

Industry observers note that the largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

According to recent reports, botPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

Industry observers note that botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

In a recent development, complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

Sources indicate that botPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

Shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Recent findings suggest that fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

It does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

[1] Yu, Qiying, et al. "DAPO: An Open-Source LLM Reinforcement Learning System at Scale." Advances in Neural Information Processing Systems 38 (2025): 113222–113244.

[2] Zhang, Shaokun, et al. "Nemotron-Research-Tool-N1: Exploring Tool-Using Language Models with Reinforced Reasoning." International Conference on Learning Representations (2026).

Sources indicate that A living trust is a legal arrangement where you (the grantor) transfer ownership of your assets to a trust entity that you also control (as trustee). It sounds circular, and in practice, during your lifetime, nothing changes about how you use your money and property. The magic happens when you die or become incapacitated.

The three key roles in a living trust:.

It has been revealed that during your lifetime: You are both the grantor and the trustee. You control everything. You can add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, modify terms, or dissolve the trust entirely. Your Social Security number is the trust's tax ID — there is no separate tax return. For practical purposes, nothing changes about your daily financial life.

If you become incapacitated: Your successor trustee immediately takes over management of trust assets. No court petition needed. No guardianship proceeding. No delay. This is a major advantage over a will, which provides zero protection during incapacity.

When you die: Your successor trustee distributes assets according to your trust document. No probate court. No public record. No waiting 6-18 months. Beneficiaries can typically receive assets within days or weeks.

In a recent development, A living trust essentially creates a private, self-executing transfer system that operates outside the court system entirely. For FI families who have spent years building wealth, this means your heirs receive the full value of your estate without probate eating into it.

It has been revealed that the terms "revocable" and "irrevocable" describe whether you can change or dissolve the trust after creating it. This distinction has major implications for control, taxes, and asset protection.

Revocable living trust — the standard choice for most families:.

It has been revealed that you retain full control. You can amend the trust, add or remove assets, change beneficiaries, or dissolve it completely at any time. Because you maintain control, the IRS treats trust assets as yours — they are included in your taxable estate, and creditors can reach them. The primary benefit is probate avoidance and incapacity protection, not asset protection or tax reduction.

Irrevocable trust — the advanced tool for specific situations:.

Once created, you generally cannot change or revoke it. You give up control of the assets placed inside. In exchange, you get benefits that a revocable trust cannot provide.

When an irrevocable trust makes sense:.

In a recent development, for most FI families: A revocable living trust is the right starting point. It provides the two biggest benefits — probate avoidance and incapacity protection — while letting you maintain complete control.

Industry observers note that creating a trust document is only half the job. A trust only controls assets that are titled in its name. An unfunded trust is a worthless piece of paper.

The re-titling process for real estate: This is the most critical step and requires recording a upcoming deed. You transfer ownership from "John Smith" to "John Smith, Trustee of the John Smith Revocable Living Trust dated January 15, 2024." Contact your county recorder's office or have your attorney prepare the deed. Most counties charge $15-$75 for recording. Notify your mortgage company (they cannot call the loan due under the Garn-St. Germain Act for transfers to a revocable trust) and your homeowners insurance carrier.

Ongoing funding discipline: Every time you open a new bank account, buy property, or acquire significant assets, ask: "Should this be titled in my trust?" Create a simple checklist and review it annually. The most common estate planning failure is a perfectly drafted trust with assets still titled in the grantor's personal name.

A common concern is whether transferring your home into a trust triggers a due-on-sale clause in your mortgage. Under the federal Garn-St. Germain Depository Institutions Act of 1982, lenders cannot accelerate a mortgage when property is transferred to a revocable trust where the borrower remains a beneficiary and occupant. This protection applies to residential properties with fewer than five units. Your lender may ask for a copy of the trust document, but they cannot call the loan. Always notify your homeowners insurance company of the title change to ensure coverage remains valid.

In a recent development, A living trust is most valuable if your net worth exceeds $500K, you own property in multiple states, you want to avoid probate, or you want incapacity protection. If your estate is simple and under $500K, a will may be sufficient.

Online services (Trust & Will $399-$599, LegalZoom $399-$599) work for simple trusts. For complex situations or estates over $1M, an estate planning attorney ($1,500-$5,000) ensures proper drafting and funding.

Your trust document should name your trustee (you), successor trustee, beneficiaries, and detailed distribution instructions. Include provisions for incapacity and specific instructions for each major asset category.

Transfer real estate by recording newly introduced deeds. Retitle bank and brokerage accounts into the trust name. Complete the assignment of personal property document. This is the most critical step — an unfunded trust is useless.

Draft a pour-over will that directs any assets not in the trust to pour into it upon your death. This will also names guardians for minor children. Review and upgrade both documents every 3-5 years.

A living trust is a legal entity you create during your lifetime that holds your assets. You serve as trustee and maintain full control. When you die or become incapacitated, a successor trustee you named manages and distributes assets to your beneficiaries — without probate or court involvement.

Recent findings suggest that A revocable living trust costs $1,500-$3,000 through an estate planning attorney, or $399-$599 through online services like Trust & Will or LegalZoom. Irrevocable trusts cost $3,000-$10,000+ due to their complexity. Additional costs include deed preparation ($200-$500) for transferring real estate.

A revocable living trust does NOT reduce estate taxes — assets are still part of your taxable estate because you maintain control. Only irrevocable trusts remove assets from your taxable estate. However, with the federal estate tax exemption at $13.61 million per individual (2024), estate taxes only affect very large estates.

According to recent reports, yes, and you should be. With a revocable living trust, you serve as your own trustee during your lifetime. You maintain complete control over all trust assets — buying, selling, spending, and investing exactly as you did before. Your successor trustee only takes over upon your death or incapacity.

A will goes through probate court (public, 6-18 months, costs 3-7% of estate). A living trust avoids probate entirely (private, days to weeks, minimal cost). A trust also provides incapacity protection, which a will does not. However, a will can name guardians for minor children, which a trust cannot.

Yes. You need a pour-over will to catch any assets not titled in the trust and to name guardians for minor children. The trust handles your major assets and avoids probate. The will serves as a safety net for everything else.

Sources indicate that A living trust is one of the most effective tools for protecting the wealth you have built on the path to financial independence. It avoids probate, provides incapacity protection, maintains complete privacy, and ensures your heirs receive assets rapidly and efficiently. The key is actually funding the trust — transferring asset titles into it. For FI families with a net worth above $500K, the $1,500-$5,000 setup cost pays for itself many times over in avoided probate fees and time savings for your heirs.

Microsoft Patches More Than 1,400 Security Flaws

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software.
  • Recent findings suggest that just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild.
  • According to recent reports, windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft today issued updates to fix more than 1,400 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and other software. Today’s epic patch batch dwarfs September’s record of nearly 1,000 fixes, which was already about ten times the normal monthly patch load from Redmond.

Recent findings suggest that just one of the weaknesses patched this week is considered a “zero day,” or already exploited in the wild. CVE-2026-96951 is a security feature bypass in the Windows Shell that affects Windows 10 and 11 systems, as well as some Server versions.

According to recent reports, windows 10 users might be wondering if they can still expect security updates after this month. Microsoft had been slated to stop shipping updates for Windows 10 systems in October 2025, but ended up adding another year of free updates after considerable pushback. A few months ago, Microsoft quietly extended that support for another year (until October 2027).

At least 78 of the flaws fixed this month are rated “critical,” meaning they could be exploited with little or no action by the user, and most of those critical bugs allow an attacker to execute code of their choice on the vulnerable system.

While Microsoft noted there are no signs anyone is exploiting it yet, a security feature bypass in the .NET Framework (CVE-2026-108398) was publicly disclosed prior to today, potentially giving attackers advance time to work out how to exploit the bug.

Satnam Narang at Tenable said the number of flaws fixed this month far surpasses the previous record-setting year 2020, when Microsoft patched 1,261 CVEs.

“We’ve now crossed the 4,000 CVE mark with two months left to go,” he stated.

Microsoft credits large language models for the high volume of bug discovery, and presumably AI gets credit for many of the patches used to fix these flaw. Meanwhile, security experts have been warning that these unusually large patch volleys from Microsoft are placing extra strain on corporate security teams, which often have to test individual updates before deploying them across a network to ensure the fixes don’t cause problems for other software.

Industry observers note that tyler Reguly, associate director of security research and development at Fortra, notes that just 26 Microsoft vulnerabilities appeared in the “Known Exploited Vulnerabilities” (KEV) catalog maintained by the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) so far this year, and security teams would do well to prioritize patching those 26 vulnerabilities first.

“Security leaders should focus on exploitable risk, and ask whether their teams have the clarity, capacity and support to act,” Reguly said.

Which vulnerabilities deserve the most scrutiny in your organization? The folks at Cisco Talos have a useful roundup of the more noteworthy flaws that Microsoft fixed today, and of course the SANS Internet Storm Center has a reliable roundup that indexes vulnerabilities by severity, CVE number and affected software.

The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2623 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
  • Sources indicate that 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
  • According to recent reports, TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

Sources indicate that 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

According to recent reports, TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

Industry observers note that A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are vital for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

LoRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

In a recent development, hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

According to recent reports, TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

Sources indicate that first, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

The sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid highlights if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

Recent findings suggest that the shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

In the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

We add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

Our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

It has been revealed that if we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Recent findings suggest that our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

In a recent development, A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

It has been revealed that the preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

This container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

According to recent reports, the training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

Sources indicate that we use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

Sources indicate that if you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

Sources indicate that the commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

In a recent development, we also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

It has been revealed that we keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

Recent findings suggest that it’s important to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We update only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

Recent findings suggest that the snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

Industry observers note that the training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

For each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

In a recent development, we trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

Recent findings suggest that the training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls quickly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

In a recent development, flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It shows the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

Industry observers note that phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

Recent findings suggest that the main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Sources indicate that gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

Thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The United Kingdom has issued economic sanctions against Cryptomus, a chameleonic cryptocurrency platform that experts say serves as a major conduit for payments related to ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud and cybercrime services that are helping Russia circumvent existing financial restrictions.

Industry observers note that heleket’s support agent on Telegram claims, despite all evidence to the contrary, that it is not affiliated with Cryptomus. Image: Richard Sanders.

Recent findings suggest that on October 8, the U.K. issued sanctions (PDF) against Cryptomus — previously known as Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises — for processing payments that benefit the Russian government and its financial institutions. The sanctions freeze any Cryptomus assets at U.K. banks, and bar British companies from offering it any business, virtual or otherwise. Also targeted in these sanctions were the virtual payment platforms VexPay, TokenSpot, and the Tsunami Payments service.

As explained in our December 2024 investigation, “How Cryptocurrency Turns to Cash in Russian Banks,” Cryptomus has been a key payment processor for dozens of Russian cryptocurrency exchanges and websites hawking cybercrime services. The company has changed its name several times since emerging in 2022, most recently to “Heleket” last year after Canada levied a record CAD $176 million fine against the platform for anti-money laundering violations.

Recent findings suggest that the blockchain data-crunching firm Chainalysis remarked the U.K. sanctions target the broader infrastructure supporting Russia’s wartime economy.

In a recent development, “Cryptomus and Heleket have emerged as major payment hubs for illicit activity,” Chainalysis wrote in an October 8 blog post. “Together, these services received more illicit funds across tracked categories than the mixers in our dataset and the number of illicit counterparties surged to more than 900 in a single month in late 2025.”.

According to recent reports, the Cryptomus support bot on Telegram, responding on Oct. 8 to an inquiry by saying the platform was suddenly unable to process transactions.

In April 2026, the blockchain analysis firm TRM Labs found Cryptomus had processed more than $7 billion in transactions since its inception in 2022, including transactions associated with child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing networks, and human trafficking operations.

TRM noted that Cryptomus’s transaction volume cratered after the platform instituted fresh “know your customer” or KYC rules, and that the cryptocurrency platform responded to the Canadian fines by launching Heleket as a parallel service that continued to offer no-KYC payment processing.

Recent findings suggest that richard Sanders is a blockchain analyst and investigator who spent months mapping out Cryptomus’s payment infrastructure and transacting with its customers. Sanders stated the U.K. sanctions on Cryptomus are notable because Canada’s fine against the platform was ultimately unenforceable and uncollectible.

According to recent reports, “A fine doesn’t stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments,” Sanders wrote on LinkedIn. “Sanctions kill the operation. The distinction matters.”.

As our 2024 investigation noted, Cryptomus shared a Vancouver address with dozens of other foreign currency dealers and money transfer businesses — none of which appeared to be physically located there. Following the CAD $176 million fine for alleged money laundering violations, Cryptomus appealed the penalty, rolled out Heleket as a parallel service, and kept on processing large volumes of sketchy transactions, Sanders stated.

Recent findings suggest that sanders mentioned the sanctions also are notable because they are the first known instance of a “Five Eyes” country (referring to the Australia, Canada, Upcoming Zealand, the U.K. and the U.S.) sanctioning a cryptocurrency operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction.

It has been revealed that where do entities like Cryptomus and Heleket derive their authority to offer international financial services? The answer appears to involve fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body positioned in a country that is not widely recognized as a sovereign nation.

Our 2024 investigation found the sole shareholder of Cryptomus’s parent tech giant Certa Payments was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed several other firms, including the WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which bills itself as the regulatory body that exclusively oversees licenses for cryptocurrency, foreign exchange and online gaming businesses incorporated in the disputed region in northwest Africa known as the Western Sahara.

Recent findings suggest that that entity’s website — crasadr.com — notes it assists applicants with bank setup and formation, online gaming licenses, and the creation and licensing of foreign exchange brokers. One of Certa Payments’ former sites — certa[.]website — also shared a server with 12 other domains, including rasd-state[.]ws, a website for the Central Reserve Authority of the Western Sahara.

The website crasadr dot com, the official website of the Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara, which lists the entities awarded licenses for cryptocurrencies, gaming and foreign exchange services.

📖 Baca

LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1707 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens.
  • Industry observers note that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models.
  • Sources indicate that today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

Industry observers note that to address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Sources indicate that today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

It has been revealed that LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

Industry observers note that the LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):.

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

It has been revealed that the role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

Sources indicate that we compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

In a recent development, safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

It has been revealed that in short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the upcoming vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

It has been revealed that tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

According to recent reports, that's really awesome! With an Apple pkl community renderer, you could potentially write PKL and render LLMON. 🥒🍋.

Any-to-pkl-community will convert json, yaml, toml to pkl, so just need the render part.

This is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. I think these technical requirements are key when estimating the cost to hire an LLM engineer, particularly for specialized enterprise projects.
